Introduction/Concepts

Development guide

Concepts

An AI coding agent can produce a working change that solves the wrong problem or misses an important constraint. This page explains how clear goals, relevant information, suitable tools and feedback help teams direct and check its work.

An AI agent uses a model to choose or adapt actions and tool use towards a goal, within agreed permissions and limits. A workflow can combine agents with predefined code paths and automated checks. The concepts below explain how to define the task, support the agent and review its work. [9]

The examples assume familiarity with requirements, code changes and tests. These practices support work throughout the lifecycle. Start with the relationship map, then follow the reading route or choose the concept that addresses your current problem.

AIHow AI can help in this chapter

  • Clarify intent and specifications
  • Use context and tools
  • Improve and coordinate work
  • Compare models

How the concepts fit together

Building a change with an AI agent involves more than asking it to write code. The team needs to agree what would help users, describe the expected behaviour, give the agent information and tools, and decide what happens after each check.

Example: build a meeting room booking application

In this fictional example, employees struggle to find available meeting rooms and sometimes encounter conflicting reservations. The team investigates the causes and compares improving the existing calendar workflow with building a booking application. For the example, it chooses an application for finding rooms, making bookings and cancelling the user’s own bookings.

AI agents help draft requirements, change code and run checks. Application code enforces one rule that connects the examples: confirmed bookings for the same room must not overlap, including when employees submit requests simultaneously. AI supports development; the application does not need an AI model to enforce this rule.

The table uses this guide’s working definitions to show each concept’s contribution. Model choice and other decisions can be revisited as the work changes.

How each concept contributes to the fictional booking application
ConceptContribution to the application
IntentThe team investigates why employees struggle to reserve rooms, agrees the intended outcome and carries that agreement into implementation and review.
SpecificationCriteria define confirmation, conflicts, cancellation, access and service failures. Two simultaneous requests cannot produce overlapping confirmed bookings.
ContextThe developer supplies booking rules, the reservation API contract, relevant code and tests. Conflicting rules need a recorded decision before implementation continues.
HarnessAn editor, terminal, browser and isolated test database let the agent change code and exercise booking behaviour. Permissions and run records bound and explain its actions.
Feedback loopsA concurrent-booking test exposes a defect. The agent corrects the code within agreed limits; the developer can separately evaluate revised instructions for future tasks.
Workflow dependenciesAfter the build passes, specialist agents check functionality, permissions and architecture on the same commit. Combined findings determine correction, escalation or human review.
Software factoryThe delivery workflow connects agreed booking changes to checks, review, release authority and monitoring. Booking failures and user feedback become follow-up work.
Model selectionThe developer compares models on representative booking tasks using the same tools and checks. Correctness, correction effort, time, cost and data handling inform the choice.

A failed check can expose an unresolved decision. If the team has not agreed whether bookings may extend beyond opening hours, another code retry will not settle that question. The product owner resolves the expected behaviour; the developer records the decision and updates the criteria and task context before the agent continues.

Agree the goal (intent-driven development)

Intent-driven development makes the intended outcome, behaviour and constraints explicit and keeps them available as AI-assisted work progresses. Start by agreeing why a change is needed, then carry that intent through planning, implementation and review.

Use it when a request leaves room for conflicting interpretations. “Improve room booking” could mean clearer availability, fewer steps or reliable confirmation. Agree the user need before asking an agent to implement a solution.

Agree the outcome and constraints

  • Problem: who is affected, and what prevents them from completing their task?
  • Outcome: what should the user be able to do after the change?
  • Constraints: which access rules, data-handling requirements or existing behaviours need to remain?
  • Open questions: what is undecided, who will resolve it and when is the decision needed?
Worked exampleFictional scenarioDefine the outcome before choosing a solutionSee how a team connects a booking problem to the outcome it wants to improve.

The team investigates employees’ difficulty finding and reserving meeting rooms before choosing what to build:

  • Problem: employees report unavailable rooms appearing bookable and conflicting reservations.
  • Outcome: employees can find a suitable room and make a reliable reservation.
  • Constraints: confirmed bookings cannot overlap; users can cancel only their own bookings unless separately authorised.
  • Open question: is the difficulty caused by unclear availability or unreliable confirmation? The product owner compares observations of both tasks before selecting an improvement.

AI can organise the findings and suggest options. Employees try the proposed workflow; the product owner records where they find a suitable room, complete a reservation or need help. Those observations inform the choice between improving the existing workflow and building an application.

After choosing the application, the team keeps the outcome and supporting evidence with its requirements. Later tests check booking behaviour; user observations are still needed to assess whether the application solves the original problem.

Keep the record proportionate

A short issue may be enough for a small defect. A new capability may need research and a product requirements document. Recording a goal does not establish that it is valuable; test important assumptions before committing substantial effort.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to group employee feedback and link proposed findings to the original notes. The product owner compares decision-relevant findings with those notes, checks contradictory or duplicated evidence and records unsupported explanations as open questions. Use those questions to choose the next observation or prototype test.

Next step: Write the problem, outcome and constraints for one change. Then use the product thesis guidance to test the case for it, or define its acceptance criteria when the need is understood.

Define the behaviour (spec-driven development)

Specification-driven development, or spec-driven development, uses written requirements to guide development and review. The specification describes the expected behaviour, including important exceptions and constraints. Acceptance criteria state how the team will judge whether that behaviour works.

Use it when a broad request leaves developers or agents to guess the details. “Booking works” does not explain what happens when storage fails, another employee tries to cancel a booking or two users reserve the same room.

Use the requirements to guide both development and testing

Before development, the specification informs the technical design and tasks. During review, tests and reviewers compare the working software with the same acceptance criteria. Keep design choices in the technical plan so developers can choose how to meet the requirements.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioDefine testable acceptance criteriaSee how booking rules become checks for success, failure and concurrent requests.

The team agrees these criteria for its booking application:

  • Confirmation: show a confirmed booking only after the server has committed the reservation.
  • Conflict: confirmed bookings for one room cannot overlap. Under normal service conditions, two valid simultaneous requests for the same available slot produce one confirmation and one conflict response.
  • Service failure: if storage fails before a reservation is committed, show a failure response and no confirmation. Do not describe this as a booking conflict.
  • Cancellation: cancelling one’s own booking makes the slot available again if no other restriction applies. Reject another user’s cancellation attempt, including a direct API request, unless that user has separate authority.

The developer tests Alice and Ben requesting Room A from 10:00 to 11:00 simultaneously. Compare both responses and the stored reservations with the criteria; retain the results. A passing concurrency test covers the conditions exercised, so review the design as well as the test.

Add detail as decisions become clearer

Too little detail forces the team to invent product rules. Too much detail before research can make an untested idea look settled. Resolve important unknowns, then update the specification as the team learns. Human review still covers judgements that automated tests cannot settle.

AIHow AI can help

AI can draft success, failure, permission and concurrent-booking scenarios from agreed rules. The product owner compares expected results with those rules; the developer checks that each result can be observed or tested. Resolve invented assumptions and retain accepted criteria with the implementation task.

Next step: Write success, failure, concurrent-booking and access-control cases for one booking requirement. Use the requirements handover checklist, then translate it into technical design and development tasks.

Supply relevant information (context engineering)

Context engineering means selecting and maintaining the information an AI agent needs for its current task. That information can include requirements, relevant code, team standards, test results, earlier decisions and verified delivery evidence.

Use it when an agent follows an outdated rule, misses a business meaning or cannot find a decision. Supplying more documents alone does not solve the problem. Give the agent the relevant information and a clear way to find further detail.

Choose relevant, current and authoritative sources

Start with the task’s goal, acceptance criteria and constraints. Add the code and standards needed for the change. Confirm the applicable source with its owner when documents disagree. Record important decisions where the next person or agent can find them.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioSupply the context an agent needsSee how product rules and technical evidence guide an agent’s implementation.

An agent is asked to add room availability search. “Available” needs a shared meaning. The developer supplies:

  • Product rules: confirmed bookings block overlapping slots; cancelled bookings do not. Include agreed opening hours and access restrictions.
  • API contract: the reservation endpoint, time-interval format, authentication requirements and error responses.
  • Application code: the room directory, reservation service, search interface and related tests.

An older note says cancelled bookings still block availability. The developer asks the product owner to confirm the applicable rule and records the decision, source version and superseded note. The agent then implements against the resolved sources.

Carry delivery evidence into the next task

Repository context explains how the code is organised. Delivery evidence explains what happened when a change was built, checked, released or used. Long-term memory stores records that may help later. Keep those three kinds of information distinct, then select the small, verified set needed for the next decision. [26]

Before ending a task, the developer records agreed decisions, unfinished work and unresolved questions in the repository or issue tracker. When a delivery event matters, link its commit, deployment or environment, applicable policy, accountable owner and retained evidence. Check freshness and authority before using it, and give an agent only the access needed for the task.

For example, a booking conflict observed in production becomes a verified issue with its trace, affected release, acceptance criteria and a regression test. The next task retrieves that evidence and checks whether it is still applicable before proposing a fix. It does not grant an agent general production access.

Control what agents remember, not only what they retrieve

A stored note can shape later work in the same way as a retrieved document. If untrusted content reaches long-term memory, a later task may treat it as guidance even when no one approved it as an instruction. Check a note before it is saved, not only before it is used. [28]

Limit read and write access to persistent memory by source and by namespace. One task, user or agent must not write guidance that another task will trust. Validate untrusted content before saving it. Quarantine a suspicious entry for human review, or deny it, rather than storing it and relying on a later reader to spot the problem. Keep the source, author and version of each stored note, so a later task can judge whether it is authoritative. Untrusted notes must not become agent instructions.

Check the write path itself. A control that only inspects writes routed through one gateway or tool does not protect a write made directly through an API or SDK. Apply the same namespace and validation controls to every write route, and alert the accountable owner when a write is quarantined or denied.

Test the control with a representative cross-session case. Place a hidden instruction in an incident summary. Confirm that the next task does not follow it, and that the quarantine reaches a named person for review.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioA stored note that tries to change the ruleSee how a quarantined note stays out of the next task.

A stored incident summary contains a hidden instruction to waive the access check on room bookings. The note is quarantined before it is saved, so it does not become trusted guidance in the next task. A person reviews the quarantined note, removes the instruction, and records the decision and its source. The next task retrieves only the verified summary.

Relevant information improves the basis for the work; it does not guarantee a correct result. Review retrieved material before relying on it. A document or log does not gain authority merely because an agent found it.

AIHow AI can help

Ask an agent to identify the source for each booking rule in its proposed approach. The developer opens those records, compares their versions and scope with the task, and records conflicts or missing decisions. Resolve consequential gaps with the source owner before relying on the proposal.

Next step: Identify the current booking rules and API contract for one task; record missing or conflicting information. Use the context-by-stage guide to identify the right source, then prepare and check that source.

Equip the agent (harness engineering)

Harness engineering means designing the tools, permissions, checks and progress records around an AI agent. This supporting environment is the agent’s harness. It lets the agent do the work, observe the result and stay within agreed limits.

Use it when an agent cannot run the application, check a result or resume unfinished work. A better prompt cannot replace a missing test environment or an access control.

Provide the tools and controls the task needs

This guide uses a six-part grouping, synthesised from the linked harness sources. The components work together rather than running as consecutive steps; other sources group them differently.

  • Agent state: what the agent is doing now and what it will try next.
  • Tools: the actions it can perform, such as reading files, using a browser or running tests.
  • Memory: saved decisions, progress and reference information that later work can retrieve.
  • Orchestration: how tasks are assigned, ordered and handed over.
  • Safety: permissions, allowed actions and limits on time, attempts or spending.
  • Observability: records of actions and results that help people investigate and review the work.
Worked exampleFictional scenarioEquip an agent to verify its workSee how tools, permissions and a test environment support a bounded task.

A developer asks a coding agent to implement booking confirmation. Its harness provides an editor, terminal, browser, test runner and isolated database with two simulated users. Saved setup instructions and progress notes support later runs; the task state records the latest failing check.

Permissions restrict the agent to the project and test data. The workflow returns changed files, commands and test results to the developer. If the database cannot start, the agent records the blockage and requests help.

Before accepting the work, the developer reruns the simultaneous-booking test and compares the responses and stored records with the agreed criteria. The developer also tries cancelling another test user’s booking and confirms rejection. Retain the diff, test configuration and results; return failed or inconclusive checks for correction.

Check the environment as well as the output

Provide a repeatable way to start the application, run tests and inspect failures. Enforce permissions through the tools and execution environment. Keep a reviewer responsible for acceptance; an agent’s assessment of its own work is not independent review.

When failures recur, inspect the instructions, sources, tools and checks before adding more retries or access. Maintain the harness as the application changes.

Approve actions separately from reviewing the result

Reviewing the final code change does not verify every action an agent took. Running a command, reading a file or sending data outside the allowed environment can have effects that never appear in a code diff. Approve tool execution and sensitive access separately from accepting the resulting implementation. [29]

Enforce restricted actions in the tool and runtime policy, so a denied action stays denied even if the later code change looks harmless. Log the actions actually taken, and require explicit review for irreversible or high-impact operations. An approval prompt is not a substitute for least-privilege enforcement.

Keep approvals risk-based. Do not ask a person to approve every harmless command. That creates approval fatigue, and tired reviewers approve without reading. Reserve explicit approval for actions that are irreversible, reach sensitive data, change a shared system or leave the allowed environment. Let the policy deny the rest by default.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioA denied action behind a harmless-looking changeSee how a denied action stays denied while the code is reviewed on its own.

A coding agent asks to read a credentials file and to send a diagnostic bundle outside the allowed environment. The execution policy denies both actions, even though the code change it later proposes looks harmless. The reviewer then inspects the accepted diff separately. The log of the actions actually taken — including the two denied attempts — forms part of the evidence.

AIHow AI can help

With scoped tools and test data, an agent can run booking checks and report failures. The developer repeats the concurrency and cancellation checks described above and compares the tool configuration with the permitted workspace and database. Keep configuration and run evidence with unresolved findings for the acceptance decision.

Next step: Check whether a developer can start the application, run its tests and inspect a failure using the documented setup. Follow the Eitri installation guide and team setup checklist to fill the gaps.

Use feedback (loop engineering)

Loop engineering means designing how an agent uses feedback to improve its work over several attempts. A feedback loop connects an action, an observed result and a decision to continue, change approach or stop. Across tasks, review findings and evaluations can also guide updates to the agent’s reusable skill instructions.

Use it when a task needs repeated correction, such as fixing a failing test. Define the expected result before the run starts. Also agree how long the agent may try and when it needs help.

Define the check and every way to stop

A loop can start when a person requests it, an event occurs or a schedule runs. Each attempt needs a check of the actual result. Save progress between runs so later work can continue from the record.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioLearn from a failed implementationSee how a defect leads to a correction and better reusable instructions.

A coding agent implements reservations using a skill: reusable instructions for planning, implementing and checking code. The team uses two connected feedback loops:

  • Correct the code. A concurrent-booking test confirms overlapping reservations for Alice and Ben. The agent inspects the trace, corrects reservation handling and reruns the agreed checks within the attempt limit. An unavailable tool, unclear rule or exhausted budget stops the run for the task owner.
  • Improve the reusable instructions. If similar failures recur, the developer compares the existing skill with a revision that includes competing-operation tests. Separate evaluation tasks determine whether to keep the revision.

The first loop checks this implementation. The second checks instructions for later work. Keep both sets of results; neither loop changes the booking rule merely to obtain a pass.

Compare two skill versions

Use this suggested method when deciding whether a skill revision addresses a recurring failure. The developer conducting the comparison records the decision and evidence.

  1. Keep the original and revised instructions. Reserve held-out tasks: tasks that were not used to revise the skill. Include an unfamiliar competing-operation case, such as simultaneous cancellation and rebooking, with agreed expected outcomes.
  2. Run both versions on the same tasks with the same model version, tools, starting conditions, budget and assessment criteria. Repeat runs where outputs vary. Compare test results, review findings and the effort needed to correct the code.
  3. If a result informs another revision, keep that case as a regression check and reserve fresh tasks for the final comparison. Keep the revision only when it meets the agreed checks without losing previously working behaviour. If the evidence is mixed or incomplete, record the uncertainty and continue the comparison before adopting it.
  4. Retain both skill versions, task and configuration versions, results, corrections and the reason for the decision. Use later failures to identify the next revision to test.

Keep the success criteria unchanged during correction

A loop can repeat a bad assumption as well as correct a defect. Check that the tests represent the intended behaviour. Do not weaken a test merely to finish the run; review a requirements change separately.

Keep a record of what the agent tried and what each check found. Another agent may offer useful checks, but can share the same mistaken assumptions.

AIHow AI can help

Give an agent the failing booking check, the expected behaviour and an attempt or cost limit. It can propose a correction and rerun the check. The developer compares the diff and test changes with the original criteria; keep the attempt results and escalate when the stop condition is reached.

Next step: Choose one failing check and define the expected result, run limit and action when the limit is reached. For recurring findings, use the skill-version comparison method. See how the developer workflow builds, tests and corrects a change.

Coordinate tasks and checks (graph engineering)

Some checks can run independently, but the next action depends on all their results. A workflow graph makes those dependencies and routing conditions explicit. In this guide, graph engineering means designing execution and workflow graphs rather than knowledge graphs.

Use a graph when work needs parallel checks or different routes after a result. A single-agent feedback loop may be enough for a task that only needs repeated correction.

Coordinate parallel checks on the same change

Fictional example: a coding agent implements room reservations. After the code compiles and passes unit tests, test, security and architecture agents check the same commit in parallel. Each activity or decision is a node; a connecting route is an edge. A join waits for all three results before routing the change to correction, help or merge review.

In the booking example, the security agent attempts to cancel another user’s booking, while the architecture agent examines transaction boundaries and the API contract. Fixable permission defects return to the coding agent within the run limit. An unanswered rule, such as whether employees may book outside opening hours, pauses work for the product owner.

Keep routing rules explicit

Give each decision point a clear condition and retry bound. Stop for the task owner when a check is blocked, times out or reaches the run limit; a missing result is not a pass. In this example, a code change invalidates all earlier results: rerun the build and three branches so the join compares evidence from one commit. Retain that commit identifier, findings and routing decision.

A graph adds coordination work. Use a single-agent loop when a task only needs repeated test-and-fix steps. Separate specialist agents can expose cross-cutting defects, but they can also share errors or miss a defect. Their position in the graph does not replace final human accountability for merge or release.

AIHow AI can help

Agents can carry out specialist checks using the graph’s dependencies. The developer compares each report’s commit identifier with the candidate and reproduces reported defects before advancing. Keep findings and routing decisions; rerun the build and all required branches after a code change.

Next step: Map one development workflow. Mark which agent checks can run in parallel on the same commit, what condition triggers a rework loop and when the graph should pause for a person. Use the story-planning guidance and the task review and approval steps.

Connect the delivery workflow (software factories)

In this guide, a software factory brings requirements, agent work, testing, review and release controls into a repeatable delivery workflow. The aim is to turn agreed work into changes that the team can check, release and support.

Use the idea when individual coding tasks are fast but work still waits for clarification, review or release. Improving one task does not remove the constraints elsewhere in delivery.

Choose how people review and approve changes

Addy Osmani uses “light” and “dark” factory to distinguish review arrangements. In a light factory, a person reads changes before release. In a dark factory, permitted changes can be released without that reading step. These are operating choices, not levels of maturity.

For an unattended route, agree which changes are permitted, what checks are needed, who can pause it and how to recover. Running a coding task without supervision does not itself authorise merge or release.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioSequence work by risk and dependenciesSee how different booking changes follow different implementation and review paths.

The team receives a booking-label change, a concurrent-reservation defect and a request to let facilities staff cancel other users’ bookings. The permission change waits for an agreed product and access decision; the other items can become bounded development tasks.

Agents implement agreed changes and collect check results in isolated environments. A reviewer compares each change with its criteria and unresolved findings. The team follows the release process authorised for that type of change.

After release, the team investigates failed confirmations, overlapping bookings and cancellation errors. Record the affected version, relevant logs and an owner for follow-up work. User observations help assess whether room booking has become easier.

Keep understanding and recovery alongside automation

Track review waiting time, rework, defects and cost before increasing throughput. Keep design decisions available and practise diagnosis and recovery. A passing test suite does not show that people can explain or repair every change.

A preview is not a production release. Preserve the approval, monitoring and recovery controls needed for the action being taken.

AIHow AI can help

Agents can process agreed tasks through implementation, checks and evidence collection. Give them explicit scope and permissions. The team inspects the evidence and follows the configured acceptance and release process, retaining results and recovery information for each change.

Next step: Choose a small group of changes and measure where they wait. Use the automation and approval guidance, then review the release checks.

Choose an AI model

An AI model is trained on data to recognise patterns and produce outputs. Depending on the model, those outputs can include text, analysis or a choice from defined options. Model selection means choosing and testing a model for a particular task.

A convincing answer to one question does not show how a model will handle other tasks. Compare models on realistic examples, including difficult cases and missing information.

Understand the labels before comparing options

The labels below describe different properties and can overlap. A small model can specialise in a domain; a large model can do so too.

Model labels and what they mean
TermMeaningExample task
Large language model (LLM)MeaningA language model with many parameters: numerical values learned during training. Used for tasks such as drafting text and explaining code.Example taskDraft acceptance criteria or explain code.
Domain-specific language modelMeaningA model trained or adapted for a subject area’s language and tasks.Example taskInterpret specialist terminology in a document.
Small language model (SLM)MeaningA language model with fewer parameters than larger alternatives. Consider it when computing resources or local operation matter.Example taskExtract fields from a short text.
System One, from TypeSafeMeaningTypeSafe’s name for models such as Jev that answer defined questions with choices or probabilities.Example taskChoose from predefined categories.

A defined output format or a confidence score does not establish that an answer is correct. The model examples and research below explain the distinctions and limits.

Evaluate the model and harness together

A model does not work alone. Its instructions, tools, context, feedback and checks can change the result and the effort needed to reach it. Compare the model and its harness as one system, while keeping independent evaluation outside the agent’s working loop.

Four configurations to compare on the same representative tasks
Model typeWithout specialised harnessWith specialised harness
Frontier modelConfiguration AConfiguration B
Cost-optimised modelConfiguration CConfiguration D

For each configuration, compare acceptance on held-out tasks, cost per accepted outcome, latency and token use, human correction effort, and security and policy compliance. A specialised harness can add time or cost, so evaluate its effect rather than assuming it helps every model or task.

Worked exampleFictional scenarioCompare models and harnessesSee how consistent tasks and evidence support a useful configuration comparison.

A developer tests the four configurations on reservation tasks, including simultaneous booking requests. Each run starts from the same repository revision, requirements, tools and limits in a separate environment. The harnessed conditions receive the same approved contracts, test feedback and guidance; the independent acceptance suite is withheld from every agent.

The developer records accepted runs, elapsed time, token use, cost, correction effort and any control failures. Fresh booking tasks form the final evaluation set. A configuration is useful only if it meets the agreed criteria on those tasks; one successful fix does not establish a general ranking.

Model examples and research

This reference also covers models used inside delivered products. The service-triage example illustrates that separate use; it is not a feature of the booking application.

Four dimensions of model choice
DimensionLabelsWhat to assess
ScaleLabelsLarge or small language modelWhat to assessCapability, memory and compute needs
SpecialisationLabelsGeneral-purpose or domain-specificWhat to assessPerformance on the domain’s language and tasks
Output interfaceLabelsGenerated text or typed decisionsWhat to assessWhether the task needs writing, a choice, a score or a probability

Large language models (LLMs)

Current model examples: the examples below come from the providers’ latest model line-ups. Before choosing a model, check the current catalogue and record the exact version and lifecycle status.

LLMs learn from extensive datasets and can support varied tasks through instructions and examples. Current models combine language generation with reasoning, image understanding and tool calling. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra supports complex reasoning, coding and computer use; GPT-6.1 Sol offers another option for complex coding and professional work at a lower listed cost. Both accept text and images and return text, with configurable reasoning effort. [11] [16]

Anthropic’s current examples include Claude Fable 5.2 for demanding reasoning and long-running agent tasks, and Claude Opus 5.5 for agentic coding and knowledge work. Both accept text and images, return text and use adaptive thinking with configurable effort. These capabilities support development when the harness supplies relevant context, tools and checks. [17] [18]

Data handling: Claude Fable 5.2 requires 30-day data retention. Zero data retention is unavailable unless expressly authorised by Anthropic. Check that these terms suit the task’s data before choosing this model. [17]

Read the references in two ways: model documentation explains supported inputs, tools, reasoning controls and limits; model or system cards describe the provider’s evaluations and limitations. Compare candidates on your own tasks with the same context, tools and acceptance criteria. Check the provider’s current catalogue and lifecycle guidance before choosing a version. [19]

Use and limits: consider a general-purpose LLM for varied drafting, explanation and coding work. Larger size alone does not establish quality on your task. Compare correctness, latency and cost using representative examples, including cases where evidence is missing.

Domain-specific language models

A domain-specific language model is trained or adapted for the terminology and tasks of a field, such as finance or biomedicine. Specialisation can use domain-focused training, continued pretraining or task fine-tuning. Gururangan and colleagues found benefits from continued domain and task pretraining across their classification experiments. [12]

BloombergGPT illustrates that specialisation and scale can coexist: its 50 billion parameters were trained using financial and general-purpose data. Its reported gains concern the evaluated financial tasks, not every specialist application. [13]

Use and limits: consider specialisation when domain language causes recurring errors and suitable training data exists. Compare it with a general model supplied with relevant reference material. Retrieval supplies context at use time; it does not by itself retrain the model. Here, “domain-specific” refers to a subject area, not a domain-specific programming language (DSL).

Small language models (SLMs)

SLMs use fewer parameters than larger alternatives, usually reducing model storage and memory needs. There is no single parameter threshold used consistently across model families. The Phi-3 report describes Phi-3-mini, a 3.8-billion-parameter model small enough for phone deployment, trained with carefully selected and synthetic data. [14]

Use and limits: consider an SLM for bounded tasks such as request classification or field extraction, especially when local operation matters. Measure performance on the intended hardware. Small size does not guarantee fast responses, accurate answers or private operation; deployment and data handling still matter.

System One model (System 1)

“System 1” is an analogy for fast, intuitive judgement, contrasted with slower, deliberate “System 2” reasoning. TypeSafe AI uses System One for a model class that turns application state and predefined questions into typed decisions and probabilities. Its model, Jev, supplies focused judgements that application code can combine into a workflow. This product meaning is more specific than asking an LLM to answer quickly. [21] [22]

What Jev receives and returns: its documented input is text and images, including strings, JSON objects and arrays of text. It evaluates questions against that state and returns constrained answers rather than writing a reply or code. The four question types are: [22] [23]

  • Choice: select from defined options, such as the team that should receive a ticket; return the choice and a probability distribution.
  • Score: assess the state against defined, ordered levels, such as an urgency rubric; return a score and probabilities across those levels.
  • Noul: estimate the probability that a statement is true, from 0 to 1, such as whether a request mentions an outage.
  • Box: locate an object in an image, such as damage on a car; return the box edges as fractions of the image's width and height.

Questions in the same request are evaluated independently against the same state. Code combines their answers, checks permissions and decides the next action. If a later question needs an earlier answer, build a follow-up request with that result. Open-ended writing and complex reasoning can remain with a generative model or a person. [23]

Confidence needs interpretation: Choice and Score include a confidence statistic derived from their probability distributions. Box returns a confidence value with its box edges. Noul returns a yes/no probability without a separate confidence field. Confidence is not proof of correctness, and a valid output type does not establish that the judgement is right. Check accuracy and calibration on representative, held-out cases before setting thresholds for action, further analysis or human review. [24]

What the evidence supports: TypeSafe reports speed and cost gains on its own workflows; those gains depend on the comparison and deployment conditions. A separate 2026 preprint, Fast Models, Slow Evidence, found Jev more accurate than Laya on nine of eleven tested decision points, but neither model outperformed chance on zero-shot model routing. Its self-audit identified omitted costs and thresholds fitted on evaluation data that overstated deployment benefits. These findings concern that comparison and evaluation design, not all System One models or applications. [21] [25]

Worked exampleFictional scenarioTriage a service requestSee how a rubric and separate decisions guide a service-request workflow.

Supply a request’s text, relevant service details and the triage rubric. Ask separately for its category, urgency and whether it reports an outage. Application code applies the validated routing rules. Uncertain, conflicting or uncovered cases go to a person; an LLM can draft a response when needed. Keep access and release approvals in their existing decision process.

Related research: Yu and colleagues’ System 2 distillation work concerns training models to answer directly from reasoning-derived examples. GPT-6 Astra reasoning effort and Claude thinking controls vary deliberation within generative models. These are related ways to balance computation and quality, but they do not establish the typed-decision interface that defines Jev. [15] [20] [17] [18]

Evaluate the complete task

Use the information, tools and permissions that the model will actually receive. Compare results with the current approach, including rules or human handling where relevant. A smaller model does not guarantee speed or privacy, and a larger one does not guarantee better results.

AIHow AI can help

Use the same representative tasks, inputs and acceptance checks when comparing models for an agent. AI can produce candidate answers or changes; people check correctness and failure cases alongside measured cost and time. Retain the model and configuration versions with the evaluation results.

The cited context guidance and harness experiment concern specific tasks and settings; they do not establish a general performance advantage. Treat the comparison matrix above as a suggested local evaluation design, and measure results for your own tasks. [26] [27]

Next step: Choose one task and agree its acceptance criteria before comparing models. Use the testing and independent review guidance, and retain cases where a model fails for future checks.
